title: Freight Logistics Internal Network: How Goods Move Through the Megacity
body:
The movement of goods through Meridian 88's interior is managed by a layered logistics infrastructure that operates largely invisibly to the city's residents while being essential to every aspect of daily life. The upper tier of this system is the automated freight corridor network — dedicated sub-street tunnels running on fixed-route autonomous freight sleds, operated under franchise by Caldor Logistics and Harmon Distribution. These corridors connect the Regional Transit Nodes to major distribution hubs located in the industrial zones at the city's periphery and in the sub-street basement levels of major commercial towers. Approximately 60 percent of the city's commercial freight volume moves through this automated tunnel system, which operates 24 hours a day with minimal human intervention.

Below the automated tier is a vast human-operated middle-distance delivery economy. Tens of thousands of workers — predominantly Tier-Three and Tier-Four, many working under gig-classification labor arrangements rather than employment contracts — operate cargo bikes, small electric vans, and hand-trolley routes through the street-level and Skywalk networks. These workers are the last-kilometer layer of the logistics system, moving goods from distribution hubs to commercial premises and residential addresses. Their labor conditions are extensively documented by worker advocacy groups and extensively ignored by regulatory bodies: variable pay tied to delivery volume, mandatory neural-uplink location tracking during shifts, liability for damaged goods deducted from earnings, and no access to the corporate health benefits available to direct employees. The 2171 Gig Labor Compact, negotiated between the major logistics operators and the Meridian Corporate Council, ratified most of these conditions as legally compliant.

The informal freight economy runs parallel to and through the gaps in the licensed logistics system. In sub-street communities and Tier-Four districts, a significant portion of goods movement occurs outside the licensed logistics architecture entirely — through informal carrier networks, neighborhood distribution cooperatives, and individual runners who move packages for flat fees. These informal logistics channels handle not just commercially-sensitive goods but ordinary necessities: food, medicine, household supplies that formal logistics operators either don't deliver to certain addresses or price prohibitively for lower-tier residents. The informal network's existence is another consequence of the formal system's calibration toward revenue-maximizing demographics.

The logistics infrastructure also serves as a significant vector for the movement of restricted or unlicensed goods, a fact that corporate security departments, MSA, and the informal networks all navigate in different ways. The automated freight tunnels have been used for contraband movement on multiple documented occasions — the sealed environment and autonomous operation create blind spots that sophisticated operators have mapped and exploited. MSA's freight enforcement division has limited resources relative to the volume of goods moving through the system daily, and its inspection protocols are largely targeted by algorithmic risk scoring rather than comprehensive review. The risk-scoring algorithms, proprietary to Caldor, have been criticized for systematic under-flagging of freight originating from corporate clients and over-flagging of goods associated with lower-tier addresses and informal economy origin points.
